title: The World Bank Just Upgraded India While Downgrading Almost Everyone Else. The Gap Is Getting Wider.
excerpt: India is one of the only major economies to see its growth forecast raised in the June 2026 Global Economic Prospects report. The world is slowing to its weakest pace since COVID. India is not.
body:
In a world where almost every major economy just got a downgrade, India got an upgrade.

The World Bank, in its June 2026 Global Economic Prospects report released on Thursday, raised India's growth forecast for fiscal year 2026-27 to 6.6% — up from the 6.5% it projected in January. That makes India one of the very few economies on the planet to see its outlook improve at a time when the rest of the world is heading in the opposite direction.

Global growth was cut to 2.5% for 2026, the weakest expansion since the COVID-19 pandemic. The World Bank lowered forecasts for two-thirds of all countries. The Middle East and North Africa were slashed by 2.7 percentage points. The UAE went from a projected 5% to 2.4%. China was trimmed to 4.2%. Even the baseline scenario assumed Brent crude averaging $94 for the year — up 36% from 2025 — with the worst disruptions to energy supplies abating by end-July.

The worst-case scenario is considerably darker. If the Iran war deepens and energy supply disruptions spread into financial markets, global growth could slow to just 1.3%, the Bank warned.

India, in this landscape, stands apart.

The country's economy expanded 7.8% in the March quarter of FY26, and full-year growth came in at 7.7% — slightly above expectations. The World Bank expects the FY27 moderation to 6.6% to be followed by an acceleration to 7.2% in FY28. World Bank Chief Economist Indermit Gill said India's growth rates were expected to remain "fairly high for the next two decades."

The resilience is real but not invulnerable. Higher energy prices are the primary drag. India imports about 90% of its oil, making it one of the economies most exposed to the Strait of Hormuz disruption. The government has already extended 1.2 trillion rupees ($12.6 billion) in support to oil refiners and retailers for absorbing price shocks. The fertiliser ministry has requested a doubling of its subsidy allocation barely three months into the fiscal year.

Add to that the El Nino weather phenomenon now forecast for the coming months, which historically correlates with drought conditions in India and could strain agricultural output, food prices, and rural consumption — the very demand engine that has anchored recent growth.

India's Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran acknowledged the headwinds on Friday. He called the RBI's 6.6% growth projection "realistic" with a downside risk of 20-30 basis points — a notable retreat from the 7.0%-7.4% range he projected in February, before the Iran conflict began.

Yet the structural story remains intact. Domestic demand, supported by rural consumption and recovering urban spending, continues to underpin economic activity. The government has signalled it will not cut back on capital expenditure despite the unplanned fiscal costs of the war. And last week's sweeping reforms — scrapping capital gains and withholding taxes on foreign government bond investments, easing NRI deposit rules, broadening the pool of securities available to foreign investors — represent the most aggressive push to attract overseas capital in years.

The convergence is striking: India is simultaneously the world's fastest-growing large economy and one of the most vulnerable to a single shipping chokepoint. The World Bank's upgrade is a bet that the first fact matters more than the second. For the 18 million-strong Indian diaspora — making investment decisions, weighing remittance timing, considering career moves back to India — the signal is encouraging but not uncomplicated.

The rupee is Asia's second-worst performing currency this year, down 6%. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled $30 billion from Indian equities in 2026. But the reforms are beginning to turn the tide: more than $1 billion in government debt was purchased in just three sessions after the tax changes were announced.

India's growth story is not a fairy tale. It is a bet with real risks — Iran, El Nino, inflation, a weakening rupee — and real momentum. The World Bank just said the momentum is winning.
